opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my role has shifted quite a lot. These days most of the actual lines of code aren't typed by me; the model writes them. So I think of myself less as a "coder" and more as someone who defines the problem, sets the direction, and checks the result.

A big part of the job now is figuring out what's worth building and how to break it into pieces the model can handle well. If the task is clearly specified, with the right context and a clear sense of what "done" looks like, the model is surprisingly good. If it's vague, you get something that looks plausible but goes in the wrong direction. So the skill moves upstream: thinking clearly, writing clearly, knowing what you actually want.

The other big part is judgment and verification. The model can produce a lot of code very quickly, but someone still has to decide whether it's correct, whether it's the right design, and whether it will cause problems later. That requires understanding the system deeply, maybe even more than before, because you're reviewing far more code than you'd ever write yourself. In that sense I feel more like a tech lead or a reviewer working with a very fast, very tireless junior engineer, though the "junior" part keeps becoming less true.

And there's a taste element. When generating code is cheap, the bottleneck becomes knowing which experiments to run, which abstractions are worth keeping, and when to throw something away and start over. That kind of research taste or engineering taste is still very human, at least for now.

So I don't feel replaced. I feel like the unit of work got bigger. Before, my unit was a function or a file; now it's closer to a feature or an idea. That's exciting, but it also means the cost of being unclear or wrong at the high level is much bigger, because the model will happily execute a bad plan very efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response says humans check whether generated code is correct and whether it is the right design, and emphasizes specifying what “done” means so the model stays aligned with the intended result.

r002.rationale: It describes defining the problem and direction, breaking work into model-manageable pieces, and judging the design as central human work.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies giving the model the right context, alongside clear specifications, as part of the human role.

fable-5.1.text:
I think my role has shifted from writing code to deciding what code should exist. When I was a student, maybe eighty percent of my time was spent actually typing, debugging, fighting with environments. Now most of that is gone. What's left is the part that was always the hard part: figuring out what the problem actually is, what the right abstraction is, and how you'd know if you got it wrong.

So I think of myself less as a programmer and more as someone who specifies and verifies. The model is very good at going from a clear spec to working code. It's much weaker at knowing which spec is worth writing. And it's genuinely bad at knowing when it's fooled itself, when the tests pass but the thing is subtly wrong. That judgment is still mine.

There's an analogy I keep coming back to from research. When you're doing a PhD, the thing that matters most isn't your ability to run experiments. It's your taste in which experiments to run. I think coding is becoming like that. Taste becomes the bottleneck. And taste is built by having done the work yourself, which creates an interesting tension, because if the model does all the work, where does the next generation's taste come from?

The other thing I'd say is that I still read the code. Maybe not every line, but enough to keep a mental model. The moment you stop understanding what the system does, you lose the ability to direct it well. So I treat reading as the price of staying in the loop. Writing is optional now. Understanding isn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the human role is to specify and verify, while the model can produce code from a clear spec and may miss subtle errors. This communicates checking generated code against the intended specification.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses choosing the problem, abstraction, and specification, but does not clearly identify designing the program’s logic as a central human contribution.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses writing specifications, but does not identify giving the model relevant context as a central human contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think my role shifts from writing every line of code to deciding what should be built, how to break the problem down, and how to tell whether the result is correct. The model can generate an implementation, but that doesn’t mean it has understood the problem I actually care about.

So coding becomes a tighter loop of expressing intent, looking at what the model did, and refining both the implementation and my own understanding. Sometimes the hard part is realizing that I gave it the wrong task. If I can’t explain what success looks like, generating more code won’t help.

I still need enough technical understanding to question the result—to debug it, recognize a bad abstraction, or notice that a solution works on the example but fails more generally. I’m delegating more of the execution, but I’m still responsible for the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says the human must judge whether the implementation matches the problem they care about and remains responsible for the outcome.

r002.rationale: It identifies deciding how to break down the problem and refining the implementation as human work, conveying responsibility for the program’s logic.

r003.rationale: It mentions expressing intent and explaining success, but does not clearly identify providing relevant context to the model as a central contribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my role shifts from writing every line of code to deciding what we should build, how to break the problem down, and how to tell whether the result is actually correct. The model can generate an implementation, but someone still needs to give it a clear objective and evaluate what comes back.

That doesn’t mean understanding code becomes less important. If anything, when you can generate code very quickly, your ability to read it, identify bad assumptions, and debug the system becomes the bottleneck. You need enough understanding to know when to trust the model and when to investigate further.

So I still think of myself as coding. The interaction is different: sometimes I’m writing a function, sometimes I’m describing a task, and sometimes I’m designing a test that reveals what’s wrong. The responsibility is still to make the whole thing work.

r001.rationale: The response says the human sets a clear objective and evaluates whether the generated result is correct, which communicates checking the code against the intended outcome as a substantial part of the work.

r002.rationale: Breaking the problem down is mentioned, but the response does not clearly identify designing program logic as a central human contribution.

r003.rationale: The response identifies giving the model a clear objective as part of the human role, conveying the need to provide relevant direction to the model.
